cards.title: What is Machine Learning?
lines: Machine learning is a process of using data to improve performance or make predictions.
A model is trained by showing it many examples of data.
Features are the input values that describe each example.
A label is the correct answer that the model is trying to predict.
Training data is used to teach the model, and test data checks how well it learned.
Pattern recognition means finding repeated relationships in a data set.

cards.title: Learning Techniques and Applications
lines: Classification sorts data into set categories, such as spam or not spam.
Clustering groups similar data together without pre-set labels.
Feedback helps improve the accuracy of a model over time.
Spam filters learn to separate wanted emails from unwanted ones.
Recommendation systems suggest items based on past user choices.
Tools like Teachable Machine let beginners train models without heavy coding.

cards.title: Core Programming Concepts
lines: A variable stores a value that can change while a program runs.
A conditional uses IF and ELSE to make decisions based on a test.
A loop repeats a block of instructions using iteration.
A function is a named block of code that performs a specific task.
Sequence, selection, and iteration are the three basic logical structures.
A flowchart or pseudocode can represent the steps of an algorithm clearly.

cards.title: Searching, Sorting and Representing Algorithms
lines: An algorithm is a finite sequence of clear steps that solves a problem.
Linear search checks each item in turn from the start; best case 1 comparison, worst case n.
Linear search works on unsorted data; binary search is faster but needs the list sorted first.
Binary search repeatedly halves the search range, so it is much faster on large sorted lists.
A sorting algorithm puts items in order, for example bubble sort comparing neighbouring pairs.
Algorithms can be represented as pseudocode (structured English) or as a flowchart (shapes and arrows).
Flowchart shapes: oval for start and stop, parallelogram for input and output, rectangle for a process, diamond for a decision.
Trace the algorithm by stepping through with sample values to check it gives the right answer.

cards.title: Sequence, Selection and Iteration
lines: The three logical structures are sequence, selection and iteration.
Sequence: steps run one after another in the order written.
Selection: a choice using IF, IF-ELSE or IF-ELIF-ELSE, based on a condition being true or false.
Iteration: repeating steps, using a FOR loop for a known number of repeats.
A WHILE loop repeats for as long as a condition stays true, so the count need not be known.
A condition evaluates to True or False, and that Boolean result decides which branch runs.
Errors to look for: a loop that never ends, an off-by-one count, or a condition using = instead of ==.

cards.title: Preparing and Cleaning Data
lines: Garbage in, garbage out: a model can only be as good as the data it is trained on.
Collect relevant data from a reliable source, then format it into a structured table.
Common errors to clean: missing values, duplicate records, inconsistent labels, obvious outliers.
Inconsistent labels such as Yes, yes and Y are read as three separate categories.
Classify each field by data type: numerical, categorical, or text.
Label every column clearly so anyone reading the file knows what it holds.
Save the prepared data in a format suitable for analysis, most commonly CSV.
Document every change made, so the preparation is reproducible and can be explained.

cards.title: Testing a Model and Measuring Performance
lines: Always test on data the model has not seen in training, or the score only measures memorisation.
Split the data into a training set and a separate test set.
Accuracy is the proportion of test examples classified correctly, given as a percentage.
Accuracy misleads on unbalanced data: predicting the majority class always can still score highly.
Precision asks what proportion of the model's positive predictions were actually correct.
Recall asks what proportion of the real positive cases the model managed to find.
Loss measures how far the outputs are from the correct answers; training reduces it.
Overfitting: training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises, so the model has memorised the examples.

cards.title: Data Types and Data Structures
lines: An integer is a whole number and a float is a number with a decimal point.
A string is a sequence of characters such as text.
A Boolean can only be True or False.
A list is an ordered collection of values that can be changed.
A dictionary stores data as key and value pairs.
A graph stores data as nodes connected by edges, useful for networks and routes.

cards.title: Rule-Based Systems and Logic
lines: A rule-based system uses set rules to make decisions.
Each rule has a condition and an action written as IF condition THEN action.
A decision tree shows choices as branches leading to outcomes.
Logical operators AND, OR, and NOT combine or reverse conditions.
A truth table lists the output for every combination of input conditions.
Rule-based systems struggle to handle uncertainty or very complex data.

cards.title: Planning and Autonomous Agents
lines: An autonomous system operates without direct human control.
An AI agent generates a plan based on its goals and available actions.
Conditional logic lets an agent choose actions based on its environment.
Sensors provide input data that influences the agent's decisions.
If the environment changes, the plan may need to be adjusted.
Examples include self-driving cars, robot vacuum cleaners, and smart thermostats.

cards.title: Presenting Data Clearly and Honestly
lines: Match the chart to the data: line graph for change over time, bar chart to compare categories.
Pie chart shows parts of a whole; scatter plot shows the relationship between two variables.
Every chart needs a title saying what it shows.
Label both axes with the quantity and its unit, for example Accuracy (%).
Add a legend or key whenever more than one series is plotted.
A chart misleads if the vertical axis does not start at zero, making small gaps look large.
Other distortions: uneven scale intervals, 3D effects, or showing only a favourable range of the data.
Read a chart by describing the trend first, then any outlier, then what it means for the model.

cards.title: Logical Operators and Truth Tables
lines: AND is true only when both inputs are true.
OR is true when at least one input is true.
NOT reverses the input: NOT true is false, NOT false is true.
A truth table lists every possible combination of inputs and the resulting output.
Two inputs give 4 rows, three inputs give 8 rows; the number of rows is 2 to the power of the inputs.
Conditions can be combined, for example IF temperature > 30 AND humidity > 70 THEN warn.
Changing AND to OR usually makes a rule fire far more often, which changes the system's behaviour.
Real AI uses these in rule-based systems, spam filters, alarm systems and decision trees.

cards.title: The AI Project Pipeline End to End
lines: Stage 1: define the problem and the intended purpose of the system.
Stage 2: collect raw data relevant to the task, from a source you can justify.
Stage 3: clean and prepare the data, and select a suitable subset for training.
Stage 4: train the model using an appropriate tool or platform.
Stage 5: test with separate data and record the performance outcomes.
Stage 6: evaluate against the intended purpose, then refine the model or the dataset.
Stage 7: deploy on an accessible platform, considering usability and who will use it.
Stage 8: document how the system works, and use version control to track changes.

cards.title: Ethical Issues in AI
lines: Bias happens when training data is unfair, leading to unfair AI decisions.
Privacy is at risk when personal data is used without informed consent.
Transparency means being able to see how an AI reached a decision.
Accountability means someone is responsible for an AI system's actions.
Facial recognition and surveillance raise concerns about personal freedom.
Developers, companies, and users all share responsibility for ethical AI use.

cards.title: Social and Personal Impact of AI
lines: AI can improve convenience and access to services such as healthcare and education.
AI may cause job displacement as machines take over some tasks.
Recommendation algorithms can influence the choices people make.
AI can affect privacy, personal data, and digital autonomy.
Different groups in society may be affected by AI unequally.
AI has both positive and negative effects at the individual and societal level.

cards.title: Building, Testing and Deploying AI Systems
lines: Building an AI system starts with defining the problem to be solved.
Data is selected and prepared before choosing and training a model.
Accuracy is a performance metric that measures how often the model is correct.
Test data must be kept separate from training data for a fair evaluation.
AI systems can be deployed as web apps, APIs, or cloud-based platforms.
Documentation and version control help others use and maintain the system.

cards.title: Comparing AI Building Tools
lines: Teachable Machine: no-code, browser-based, trains image, audio or pose models very quickly.
Machine Learning for Kids: trains a model then plugs it into Scratch blocks for a working program.
Scratch with AI extensions: block-based, good for showing logic and conditions visually.
Google Colab: writes real Python with TensorFlow, full control and detailed metrics, steeper to learn.
No-code tools are faster to a working result and keep the focus on the AI process.
Code gives control over the model, the parameters and the metrics, and teaches transferable skills.
For a school project, build a baseline with a no-code tool first, then rebuild in code and compare.
Comparing two tools in the report is itself good evaluation material.

cards.title: Risks of AI and Differing Viewpoints
lines: Commonly named risks: bias, loss of jobs, loss of privacy, misinformation, over-reliance, lack of accountability.
Different groups judge these risks differently and with different urgency.
Developers often stress the benefits and argue that problems are technical and solvable.
Workers and unions stress job displacement and the pace of change.
Governments and regulators focus on safety, accountability and who is liable when AI causes harm.
Optimistic view: AI removes dull work, speeds up medicine and science, and creates new kinds of jobs.
Cautious view: benefits are unevenly shared and harms fall hardest on those with least power.
A good answer presents more than one perspective, supports it with a real example, and acknowledges genuine disagreement.

cards.title: Collaboration and Documentation
lines: Agree roles and responsibilities at the start so each member owns a clear part.
Use a shared platform to store files, code and datasets so everyone has the same version.
Record project steps, decisions and changes in an organised format as you go.
Version control keeps a history of changes so you can undo a mistake and see who changed what.
Documentation should state the purpose, the process, the data used and the results.
Communicate clearly and respectfully, and hold short regular progress check-ins.
Reflect at the end on both group performance and individual contribution.
Present the final project in a format suitable for review or assessment.
